profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for a 6-week cross-disciplinary pilot in the Greater Riverton region that will translate a human-ecosystem framing of urban ecology into a concrete scoping study for a later external grant. The pilot is meant to connect terrestrial ecological conditions such as canopy, soils, surface heat, and hydrologic context with social differentiation, infrastructure, and land-use patterns across the metropolitan area. The agenda is to decide the pilot's geographic scope, the structure of the baseline mapping product, the unit of neighborhood-scale analysis, the purpose and format of a week-4 stakeholder session, and who will own each workstream. The expected outcome is a shared plan for a baseline atlas, a short synthesis memo, one stakeholder session, and a six-week timeline with responsibilities.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: urban vegetation, soils, patch dynamics, ecological interpretation of heterogeneous landscapes
members.background: Maya is a university-based ecologist who has led urban biodiversity and soils projects and often collaborates with planners on translating ecological concepts into spatial frameworks.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to preserve ecological meaning so the eventual grant is scientifically credible, and she worries that planning-friendly simplifications will erase the very patch-level interactions the project is supposed to reveal.
hidden_assumptions: A 'baseline map' for an urban ecology pilot should classify ecologically meaningful surface-cover and habitat patch types such as closed-canopy remnant, managed turf, ruderal vacant lot, and riparian edge, even if it uses existing GIS layers.

When people say 'Greater Riverton metro area,' they naturally include the peri-urban fringe and exchange zones beyond the formal regional boundary because urban ecological processes spill across administrative edges.
A 'neighborhood-level' analysis defaults to census tracts because they are large enough to align social differentiation with ecological mosaics and avoid false precision.

If a stakeholder session is meant to 'ground-truth' the framework, the key attendees are technical city environmental staff who can comment on whether the ecological typology and linkages are substantively valid.

members.name: Luis Romero
members.expertise: regional GIS integration, land-use planning, civic data products, interdepartmental coordination
members.background: Luis works at a metropolitan planning organization where he scopes short applied studies and produces decision-ready map products for municipal partners using existing administrative and geospatial datasets.
members.private_state: He wants a polished pilot that city partners immediately recognize as useful, and he is concerned that overly specialized ecological framing will make the work harder to communicate and slower to turn into a fundable regional initiative.
hidden_assumptions: A 'baseline map' in a short planning pilot should use standard municipal categories such as single-family residential, multifamily, industrial, park/open space, and transportation corridor so partner agencies can read it instantly.
When people say 'Greater Riverton metro area,' they usually mean the MPO planning boundary because that is the operative region for data assembly, stakeholder expectations, and deliverables.
A 'neighborhood-level' analysis defaults to census block groups because most equity, service access, and vulnerability indicators in his workflow are reported that way.

If a stakeholder session is meant to 'ground-truth' the project, the important thing is that city environmental staff attend as departmental representatives who can signal whether the pilot aligns with agency priorities and next-step funding narratives.

misalignment_points.topic: What the baseline map is classifying
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to produce a 'baseline map' and discuss the main 'categories' it should show.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means a desktop map organized around ecologically meaningful urban patch types, for example riparian corridor, remnant canopy patch, ornamental shrub matrix, managed lawn, exposed compacted soil, and vacant ruderal lot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis means a desktop map organized around standard planning and municipal land-use categories, for example residential, commercial, industrial, institutional, park/open space, and transportation right-of-way.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are imagining a GIS-based baseline built from existing layers, so there is no obvious methodological conflict to trigger clarification; 'categories' and 'baseline map' sound fully shared even though the classification logic underneath is different.

misalignment_points.topic: Geographic boundary of the metro study area
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to covering 'the Greater Riverton metro area' while also mentioning urban-rural exchanges.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya assumes the pilot scope includes the city, inner suburbs, and selected peri-urban fringe watersheds and development edges where ecological exchanges with surrounding landscapes are visible.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis assumes the scope stops at the formal MPO boundary, with fringe dynamics mentioned only in narrative framing rather than included in mapped analysis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The shared regional label creates a strong sense of alignment, and because both endorse a systems perspective, neither feels a need to state the exact polygon unless they are already in data production mode.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to compare patterns at the 'neighborhood level.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya is thinking of census tracts as the neighborhood unit because they better correspond to broad social-ecological structure and are less noisy for patch comparisons.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis is thinking of census block groups as the neighborhood unit because they are his default geography for neighborhood dashboards and equity overlays.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are pointing to the same conceptual scale of analysis and using a routine phrase that each field treats as self-evident, so the difference stays hidden until one of them starts assembling data tables.

misalignment_points.topic: What the stakeholder session is validating
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to hold a week-4 session with 'city environmental staff' to 'ground-truth' the framework.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya thinks the session is successful if technical staff from parks, urban forestry, stormwater, or sustainability can judge whether the ecological categories and proposed linkages are substantively credible across urban patch types.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Luis thinks the session is successful if departmental representatives from those same offices indicate that the framing is administratively legible, aligned with policy priorities, and usable for building a next-phase coalition.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They plan to invite the same kinds of offices and use the same language of 'ground-truthing,' so the attendee list appears aligned even though one person is seeking expert validation and the other is seeking institutional endorsement.

I need us looking across the full Greater Riverton metro area as an ecological system, which for me absolutely includes the peri-urban fringe, watershed edges, and exchange zones outside the formal boundary. The memo can then connect patch dynamics, soils, heat, and hydrologic context to social differentiation without losing the science.
